title: Einstein--Langevin source correlations in closed non-relativistic systems
abstract: Stochastic semiclassical gravity represents stress--energy fluctuations through the Einstein--Langevin noise kernel. We examine its Newtonian projection for specified closed, particle-number-conserving non-relativistic sources and distinguish the source covariance from a reduced matter channel. The connected one-particle covariance is state dependent and differs from the universal potential-noise law postulated in the Diósi--Penrose model. To relate the source spectrum to dephasing, we define a separate static probe subject to a prescribed Gaussian noise law. For a finite-variance source operator in an isolated non-degenerate eigenstate, the full connected spectral measure has a gap around zero. The probe dephasing exponent is then bounded and its long-time slope vanishes. Stationary doublets can instead carry static or low-frequency spectral lines, while a specified freely spreading Gaussian source gives a finite limiting exponent. Continuum results depend on preparation, normalisation, infrared regularisation and the order of limits. We also compare coherent and incoherent many-body preparations and establish no-signalling for fixed classical-noise channels. These results identify the spatial, temporal and dynamical assumptions needed to relate source fluctuations to a matter-decoherence model. They do not exclude Markovian limits in other number-conserving non-relativistic preparations.
summary: This theoretical work analyzes source correlations in non-relativistic quantum systems coupled to gravity using the Einstein–Langevin formalism. The authors demonstrate that the resulting source covariance differs from the universal predictions of the Diósi–Penrose model. The findings establish stringent conditions on the source and probe dynamics required to relate source fluctuations to matter decoherence.
main_problem: The paper investigates the relationship between source fluctuations in closed non-relativistic quantum systems and the resulting matter-decoherence model, specifically comparing derived source covariance to predictions from the Diósi–Penrose model.
main_result: The connected one-particle covariance is shown to be state-dependent and differs from the universal potential-noise law postulated in the Diósi–Penrose model, and the long-time dephasing slope vanishes for certain preparations.
method: The authors use the Einstein–Langevin framework to calculate the source covariance, analyze spectral measures, and examine the decay of coherence using various source preparations (e.g., localized free sources, stationary doublets).
model_or_system: The system involves closed, particle-number-conserving non-relativistic sources coupled to gravity, analyzed via the stochastic semiclassical gravity approach. The analysis compares the derived source spectrum to the predictions of the Diósi–Penrose model.
key_observables: Connected one-particle covariance, source spectral measure, probe dephasing exponent, and the long-time slope of the dephasing rate.
important_parameters: Finite-variance source operator, isolated non-degenerate eigenstate, and the specific noise law prescribed for the static probe.
main_assumptions: The analysis requires specifying the source covariance, gravitational response, and probe dynamics separately; continuum results depend on preparation, normalization, and the order of limits.
figures_summary: Figure 1 provides a schematic summary of equal-time and unequal-time results, and Table I compares derived and unsmeared DP potential-noise kernels.
paper_structure: The paper develops the source covariance calculation, compares it to the DP model, analyzes the spectral properties for different source preparations (eigenstate, Gaussian), and concludes by establishing the necessary assumptions to link source fluctuations to matter-decoherence.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous theoretical framework for understanding how quantum gravity fluctuations (modeled via EL noise) manifest as decoherence, offering concrete, testable predictions that challenge universal assumptions found in simpler models like the DP model.
